summary: Teach angle estimation as the sense-making partner of protractor measuring: the child judges an angle's size in degrees WITHOUT a tool by comparing it to internalised benchmarks (45°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). The goal is a stable mental image of a right angle, a straight angle and a three-quarter turn, so any angle can be placed relative to them ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°'). This extends acute/obtuse vocabulary to REFLEX angles (between 180° and 360°), met here for the first time and not directly readable on a semicircular protractor. Estimation makes measuring self-correcting: a child who expects 'about 130°' will not accept a protractor read of 50°.
misconceptions: Judges size by ray length rather than opening, so estimates a wide-but-short angle as smaller than a narrow-but-long one (arm-length carryover).
Has no reflex concept — sees a 270° reflex angle and reads/estimates the smaller 90° companion instead.
Anchors only to 90° and 180°, so estimates cluster at right angles and straight lines with poor resolution in between (e.g. calls everything obtuse '120°').
Treats 'estimate' as 'measure without care' and expects an exact answer rather than a reasoned approximate range.

activities.title: Predict-then-reveal angle estimation trainer
steps: Look at an angle shown in a random orientation and, BEFORE any measuring, commit an estimate of its size in degrees (set a slider or type a number).
In ordering rounds, drag four angles into order from smallest to largest by eye before anything is measured.
Reveal the true measure and your error; when offered, fade in a faint benchmark 'ghost' (right-angle corner, or 180° straight line) over the angle to see how your estimate compared.
Meet angles whose ray (arm) lengths are varied at random so a wide angle sometimes has short arms — estimate by the opening, not the line length.
Meet reflex angles that swing past the straight line, and estimate them as 360° minus the smaller companion angle.
activities.insight: Any angle can be placed relative to a small set of benchmarks, and reflex angles (between 180° and 360°) are real angles estimated as 360° minus their companion — not the smaller angle on the other side.

activities.title: Scored estimation and classification practice
steps: Use a slider to estimate a shown angle's degrees, aiming to land within a tolerance band.
Order four angles smallest-to-largest by eye as an ordering task before any measure is shown.
Classify shown angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex, and pick out the reflex angle in a diagram.
Tackle at least one deliberately short-armed, wide-opening item designed to catch the arm-length habit.
activities.insight: Relative judgement (which is bigger), absolute estimation (how many degrees) and classification (acute/obtuse/reflex) are distinct skills that can each be practised and checked.

activities.title: Benchmark-angle gallery with everyday referents
steps: Tap or reveal each benchmark in turn — 45° (half a right angle), 90° (right angle/corner/quarter turn), 180° (straight), 270° (three right angles), 360° (full turn) — and link it to a reference image.
Connect each benchmark to a bodily or everyday referent: clock hands, an opening door, a ramp, a turn.
Use a lift-the-flap or 'more or less than a right angle?' layer to decide, for a shown angle, whether it is above or below the corner benchmark.
activities.insight: A small set of benchmark angles, anchored as physical and mental images, is the master reference set against which every other angle is judged ('a bit more / a bit less than a corner').

activities.title: Add intermediate anchors to sharpen resolution
steps: For a learner whose estimates snap only to 90° and 180°, bring in the half-right-angle (45°) and 'a right angle plus a third of a right angle' (120°) as working anchors alongside the secure 90° and 180° images.
Estimate angles that deliberately sit BETWEEN benchmarks, such as 60°, 110° or 130°, naming the two anchors each one falls between.
Justify at least one estimate aloud with benchmark language ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°').
activities.insight: Anchoring only to 90° and 180° makes estimates cluster there with poor resolution in between; deploying intermediate anchors gives the mental ruler finer gradations.

checkQuestion: Lay out four angles the child can see but not measure — include one clearly acute (~40°), one obtuse (~130°), one drawn with short arms but a wide opening, and one reflex (~270°), with ray lengths deliberately uneven. Say: 'Without measuring, put these in order from smallest to largest, and tell me roughly how many degrees each one is.' Then let them measure to check. Watch the ordering and the estimates — do not coach.
checkAnswer: Orders the four correctly by opening (not by arm length), estimates each within roughly ±15° of its true size, classifies the ~270° one as reflex (over a straight line, under a full turn) rather than reading its 90° companion, and uses benchmark language ('a bit more than a right angle') to justify at least one estimate.
